1.x: Jesus comes down from the mountain after finishing his Sermon on the Mount.

5.x: A Centurios was an officer in the Roman army, typically commanding 100 men (from the Latin “Centum” meaning 100). He was the backbone of the Roman military machine and, to the Jews, a symbol of pagan occupation. The Centurion asks for a miracle. Jesus, instead of rebuking the man for being a soldier for an oppressive empire, he says “I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel” (v 10). Jesus commends the man’s faith as the highest example of belief. Throughout the NT we see interactions between leaders of the faith and military personnel. In no instance is a soldier told that they must resign from the military to follow God. When soldiers came to John the Baptist asking how they should live a life of repentance, John gave them specific ethical guidelines but did not tell them to quit the Army: “Do not take money by force or false accusation,” he said. “Be content with your wages” (Lk 3:14 BSB). If military service were inherently sinful, John would have commanded them to lay down their sword. Instead, he commanded them to be just and content within their profession. In Acts 10, the first non-Jew to receive the Holy Spirit and be baptized was Cornelius, a Centurion of the “Italian band.” When the Apostle Peter arrived to preach to him, Peter did not tell him to leave the Roman legion. He baptized him as he was. Paul frequently used military service as a high-honor metaphor for the Christian life. He didn’t view the military as a “necessary evil,” but as a model for discipline and sacrifice: “Thou therefore endure hardness,as a GOOD SOLDIER of Jesus Christ. No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affair of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a SOLDIER” (2 Tim 2:3-4 KJV). The NT teaches that the State has a God-given mandate to maintain order, which includes the use of force (the military and police): “For he(the State) is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he BEARETH NOT THE SWORD IN VAIN: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4 KJV). Paul identifies the soldier (the one bearing the sword) as a “minister of God” for the purpose of restraining evil and protecting the innocent.

10.x: “he marvelled”: the Greek word for “marvelled” is ethaumasen. In the gospels, Jesus is only recorded as “marvelling” twice: once at the unbelief of His own people (Mk 6:6) and here at the faith of a gentile soldier.

11.x: “Many shall come from the east and west”: This refers to the Gentiles from across the globe. “Sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob”: Jesus is stating that these “outsiders” will have equal status with the Jewish Patriarchs in eternity.

12.x: This verse is a stern warning to those who believe their lineage or religious heritage guarantees them a spot in heaven. The “children of the kingdom” are the Jews. “Outer Darkness”: a place of exclusion from God’s presence: “They will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction, SEPARATED from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might” (2 Thess 1:9 BSB). “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” refers to an expression of intense regret and sorrow. Jesus is teaching that faith, not ancestry, is the entry requirement for the Kingdom.

13.x: “as thou hast believed”: Jesus grants exactly as the Centurion believed. Jesus made sure the Centurion knew it was based on his faith, and not on his actions.

16.x: “When the even was come”: this detail is more than a time stamp. Because the previous healing (Peter’s wife’s mother) took place on the Sabbath (Mk 1:29-31 & Lk 4:38-39 specify it happened right after gathering at the Synagogue, which is held on the Sabbath), the people waited until sunset (the official end of the Sabbath) to carry their sick to Jessus without violating traditional travel restrictions. “With his Word”: Jesus is the Word of God (Jn 1:1). However, he is not a second divine eternal divine person. Jesus is an authentic human being in whom God the Father dwelt (Col 2:9-10; 2 Cor 5:19; 1 Tim 2:5), hence, the Words of Jesus (when speaking as God) are the Father’s: “For I have not spoken of myself(from my humanity); but the Father which sent me(into the world, just like He sent John), He gave me a commandment, WHAT I SHOULD SAY, AND WHAT I SHOULD SPEAK” (Jn 12:49 KJV) & “Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? THE WORDS THAT I SPEAK unto you I speak not of myself: but THE FATHER THAT DWELLETH IN ME, he doeth the works.” (Jn 14:10 KJV). Jesus did not need to do rituals or incantations, His Word had the authority of God(the Father) Himself.

17.x: Matthew quotes Isa 53:4 to explain that Jesus’ healings were not just random acts of kindness, but the fulfillment of the “Suffering Servant” prophecy of Isaiah 53. “Took” (elaben): To seize or take away. “Bare” (ebastasen): To carry as a burden.

18.x: Jesus was getting overwhelmed by the large crowds, so he had to escape to the other side of the Lake. This refers to crossing the Sea of Galilee from Capernaum to the region of Gadarenes/Gerasense (there is a variant in the specific name).

23.x: After these hard sayings, Jesus enters the ship. Matthew notes that “his disciples followed him.” This acts as a separator: many heard the cost, but only a few actually stepped into the boat. Jesus is not looking for fans or casual observers; he is looking for disciples who are willing to sacrifice their comforts and their traditional identities for the sake of the gospel.

24.x: “a great tempest”: the storm is “great” (seismos, the same word for earthquake). The cost of discipleship discussed in the previous verses is immediately put to the test. This miracle demonstrates that Jesus’ authority is not just over sickness and demons, but over the very laws of nature. The Sea of Galilee is known for sudden, violent storms due to its geography. Jesus is “asleep” through the tempest. He was physically exhausted from dealing with the large crowds. Jesus, as the Son (authentic human being): (1) was born a baby (Lk 2:7); (2) grew mentally, physically, spiritually, and socially (Lk 2:52); (3) was tempted by the devil (Lk 4:2); (4) hungered (Mt 4:2); (5) thirsted (Jn 19:28); (6) Grew weary (Jn 4:6); (7) Slept through a storm (v 24); (8) prayed (Lk 22:41); (9) was scourged and beaten (Jn 19:1-3); (10) died (Mk 15:37); (11) was sacrificed for sins (Heb 10:10-12); (12) did not know all things (Mk 13:32); (13) had no power (Jn 5:30); (14) was inferior to God (Jn 14:28); (15) was a servant (Phil 2:7-8). Since Trinitarians see the Son as the 2nd divine person of the Trinity that is God as well, they use Phil 2:6-8 to argue that God-the-Son “emptied” himself and made himself of no reputation, submitting, willingly, to the Father. If that’s true, then God-the-Son essentially ceased to be God, since Jesus no longer had the divine attributes of omniscience, omnipresence, etc. The Oneness position understands the authentic humanity of the Son VS the divinity of the only divine person, the Father (aka the Holy Spirit, which was the one that conceived baby Jesus in Mary’s womb).

25.x: The ship has often been seen as a symbol of the Church (from the Greek ekklesia, which means assembly or congregation of believers and DOES NOT mean a human institution nor a physical building). We are the temple of God (1 Cor 3:16). “For where TWO or THREE are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mt 18:20 KJV). God “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Acts 17:24 KJV). So the idea that “Church” means a Latin Roman human institution is just completely unbiblical. These verses can represent the waves hitting the Church, yet the presence of Christ ensures its safety (Mt 16:18).

26.x: Before Jesus addresses the strom, he addresses the disciples. Their fear was an indicator of “little faith” (oligopistos). To Jesus, if he is in the boat (the Church), the destination is guaranteed. Faith is not the absence of the storm, but the presence of peace in the midst of it. Jesus “rebuked” (epetimēsen) the winds and the sea. This is the same word used when he rebukes demons. It suggests that he is speaking ot the creation with the voice of the Creator. “Great Calm”: usually, after a wind stops, the water remains choppy for hours. Here, the calm was as “great” as the storm had been: instantaneous and absolute.

27.x: In Jewish thought, only God had the power to still the raging sea: (1) "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still." (Ps 107:29 KJV); (2) "Thou rulest the raging of the sea: when the waves thereof arise, thou stillest them." (Ps 89:9 KJV). By performing this miracle, Jesus was revealing his divinity. The disciples were beginning to realize that Jesus was not just a teacher or a prophet.

28.x: If you look at a map, you will see that Gergesa is on the other side of the Sea of Galilee across from Capernaum. However, there is a variant. The Majority Text & Textus Receptus read “Gergesenes”, but the Critical Text reads “Gadarenes”, referring to Gadara. The parallel accounts of this verse (Mark 5:1 & Luke 8:26) also have variants. TR & MT read “Gadarenes” in Mark & Luke, while the CT reads “Gerasenes.” Harmonizing all three parallel verses, the most common rendering is “Gadarenes”. Gadara was a major city in the Decapolis. “Country of the [Gadarenese]”: it could refer to the region in general, not just the city itself, since the city is miles deeper into the land (5-6 miles from the Sea of Galilee). However, some prefer “Gergesenes” because it is a coastal village, and the story needs a steep bank into the water (pigs rushing into the sea). If “Gergesenes” was original, scribes unfamiliar with it might have replaced it with “Gadarenes” (a famous city), but many scholars argue it is a Scribal “correction” rather than the original wording, since the oldest (but fewer) manuscripts read “Gadarenes.”

2-4.x: Jesus performs his first recorded miracle after descending from the Sermon on the Mount. Leprosy in the ancient world was more than a disease; it was a social and religious death sentence. Lepers were required to cry “Unclean!” and stay at a distance. This man breaks protocol to “worship” Jesus. In his prayer, he does not doubt Jesus’ power (“thou canst”), only his willingness (“if thou wilt”). According to the Law, touching a leper made a person ceremonially unclean (Lev 13). However, when Jesus touches the leper, the “cleanness” flows from Jesus to the man, rather than the “uncleanness” flowing to Jesus. He is the only one who can touch the untouchable without being defiled. In v.4, Jesus commands the man to follow the specific instructions found in Lev 14. This serves as a “testimony” to the priests that a miracle has occurred. Here is what the mad had to do once he reached the priest: (1) The Examination (Outside the camp): The priest had to go outside the city to meet the man. He would examine the skin to ensure the “plague of leprosy” was truly gone. (2) The Two Birds: The man had to provide two live, clean birds. One bird was killed over running water in an earthen vessel. The living bird, along with cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop, was dipped in the blood of the dead bird. The priest sprinkled the blood on the healed man seven times and released the living bird into the open field (symbolizing the man’s freedom). (3) Personal Cleansing: The man had to wash his clothes, shave off all his hair (including eyebrows), wash his body in water, & wait seven days before fully re-entering his tent. (4) The Sacrifice (Day 8): On the 8th day, the man offered two he-lambs and one ewe-lamb (or birds if he was poor). Also a meat (grain) offering mingled with oil. The priest took the blood of the trespass offering and put it on the right ear, the right thumb, and the right big toe of the healed man: dedicating his whole being back to God’s service. Jesus commanded all this to: (1) Validate the Miracle: Only God heal leprosy. By sending the man of the priest, Jesus was forcing the religious leaders to document a miracle that only the Messiah was expected to perform. (2) To Restore the Man: Without the priest’s declaration, the man remained a social outcast. Jesus wanted him fully restored to his family and the community of faith. (3) To Fulfill the Law: Jesus proves he did not come to “destroy the Law, but to fulfil” (Mt 5:17). He stayed within the legal framework God had established through Moses.

Catholicism sees the Sacrament of Penance in these verses. The Ignatius Catholic Study Bible states: “Jesus’ cleansing of the leper signifies the Sacrament of Reconciliation. Leprosy represents mortal sin, the spiritual disease that extinguishes grace from the soul and impedes one’s full participation in the Church. This condition can also be contagious and influence others through scandal and false contrition. The Levitical priest typifies New Covenant PRIESTS(Catholic priests), who are instrumental in reconciling sinners with God and restoring them to spiritual health through the sacrament.” (Study notes on Mt 8:4). This however, is not Biblical. Catholicism is placing human mediators between men & God, and Jesus specifically came to replace that OT system. The Bible clearly teaches: (1) the Levitical priesthood is fulfilled/replaced in Christ; (2) believers share in a “royal priesthood”; and (3) church leaders like elders/overseers exists, but NOT AS MEDIATORS LIKE THE OLD PRIESTS. The Levitical priesthood is replaced by Christ: “For the priesthood being changed, there is made of necessity a change also of the law.” (Heb 7:12 KJV); “They truly were many priests… But this man, because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood.” (Heb 7:23-24 KJV); “Every priest standeth daily… offering oftentimes the same sacrifices…But this man… offered one sacrifice for sins for ever…” (Heb 10:11-12 KJV). The Levitical priesthood is no longer needed because Jesus fulfills and replaces it. Jesus is the ONLY High Priest and mediator between God & men: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” (1 Tim 2:5 KJV); “We have a great high priest… Jesus…Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace…” (Heb 4:14-16 KJV). No human replaces Christ, he is the only mediator, we can now “come boldly unto the throne of grace” through Christ without a human mediator. Now all believers become a royal priesthood for God: “Ye also… are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices…” (1 Peter 2:5 KJV); “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood…” (1 Peter 2:9 KJV); “He hath made us kings and priests unto God…” (Rev 1:6 KJV). The priesthood is no longer a special tribe, it includes all believers for SPIRITUAL SACRIFICES since sins are already forgiven through the one sacrifice of Christ (Heb 9:26-28; 10:12-14). Examples of these “spiritual sacrifices” are: (1) “present your bodies a living SACRIFICE, holy acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Rom 12:1 KJV); (2) “therefore let us offer the SACRIFICE OF PRAISE to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name” (Heb 13:15 KJV); (3) “to do good and to communicate(share) forget not: for with such SACRIFICES God is well pleased” (Heb 13:16 KJV); (4) “The SACRIFICES of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps 51:17 KJV); (5) Paul refers to the financial gifts from the Philippians as “an odour of a sweet smell, a SACRIFICE acceptable, wellpleasing to God” (Phil 4:18 KJV), etc. Therefore there will be no more actual sacrifices for sin because the “once for all” sacrifice of Jesus was perfect, the repetitive animal sacrifices of the OT were rendered obsolete: "Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin." (Heb 10:18 KJV). Also, the Bible establishes a blood-covenant principle: sin leads to death, and therefore life (represented by blood) must be given to cover that sin: “without shedding of blood is no remission” (Heb 9:22 KJV) & “For the life of the flesh is in the blood... for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul” (Lev 17:11 KJV). This means that the Catholic Eucharist CANNOT be a sacrifice for sins. And since there are no more sacrifices for sin, there is no more need for a human priest. That’s why in the NT, the leadership of the Church is done by elders and overseers (not mediators): “They ordained them elders in every church…” (Acts 14:23 KJV), “Ordain elders… for a bishop(overseer) must be blameless…” (Titus 1:5-7 KJV), “Feed the flock of God…Neither as being lords over God’s heritage…” (1 Peter 5:2-3 KJV); “ordain elders in every city… if any be blameless, the HUSBAND OF ONE WIFE, HAVING FAITHFUL CHILDREN not accused of riot or unruly” (Titus 1:5-6 KJV). The point is that leaders exist (elders/bishops,overseers), but they are shepherds/teachers, not sacrificial priests. No more human mediators are needed because of Christ: “Having therefore… boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus…” (Heb 10:19-22 KJV). In the OT, only priests could approach God. In the NT, ALL believers have direct access. When Jesus died, the veil (or curtain) was torn in the Temple in Jerusalem, specifically the curtain that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place (Holy of Holies) (Mt 27:50-51). The tearing happened from top to bottom, symbolizing it was God’s action, not man’s. And it signified that access to God was now opened. The old priestly barrier was removed. This connects directly with Heb 10:19-20 (KJV): “Having… boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus… through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.” As the Eucharist began to be treated more and more as a SACRIFICE instead of a MEMORIAL, by the 200s AC, Tertullian calls “elders”(presbyteros in Greek) as “sacerdos” (priest) in Latin for the first time (On Baptism, Ch 17, ~200). He is an early step toward LATER Catholic/Orthodox priesthood language, but not the fully developed version yet. Early Christiniaty specifically stood out from Judaism with its lack of priests. The Jews had the temple (destroyed in 70AC), had priests, and had sacrifices. On the other hand, Christians had no temple, no sacrifices, no priests, and met in homes.

6-9.x: The Centurion comes to Jesus not for himself, but on behalf of his paralyzed servant, showing the quality of his heart. In the Roman Empire, a servant (pais in Greek, which can mean child or slave) was often viewed as disposable property. Yet, this Centurion is deeply distressed by his servant’s suffering and goes to great lengths (even risking social stigma by approaching a Jewish teacher) to seek help. The directors of the TV show “The Chosen” assumed this servant was a bastard of the Centurion. Though a man of high rank, the Centurion exhibits extraordinary humility and says: “I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof.” He recognizes that Jesus’ holiness is of a different order than his own military status. He also deduced that if he can command action from a distance simply by giving an order, then Jesus (who is clearly operating under the ultimate authority of God) can command sickness to leave just by speaking a word. Jewish tradition held that a person who entered a Gentile’s house was ceremonially defiled (Jn 18:28). The Centurion, undoubtedly familiar with this law, felt unworthy of having Jesus suffer such an inconvenience for his sake. He also had faith enough to know that Christ could heal from a distance by merely speaking a word.

14-15.x: “his wife’s mother”: Peter was married (1 Cor 9:5), he was neither celibate, nor a Roman Pope. In fact, Paul teaches that: “A BISHOP then must be blameless, THE HUSBAND OF ONE WIFE, vigilant, sober…” (1 Tim 3:2 KJV). The idea that Peter was in Rome early as a Bishop (Pope) comes from an error that Justin Martyr made in his “First Apology.” Justin says that in Rome there was a statue with the inscription: “Simoni Deo Sancto” (To Simon the holy god”). He believed the statue was dedicated to Simon Magus (the person that tried to buy Holy Spirit power in Acts 8:18). Later archaeological evidence showed that the inscription actually read: “Semoni Sanco Deo,” referring to “Semo Sancus”, an ancient Roman god, not Simon Magus at all. This error caused many Christians the impression that Simon Magus was honored as a god in Rome. This contributed to later apocryphal books about Peter going to Rome to confront Simon Magus, in which dramatic miracles and contests between the two occur. This also led later Christians to believe that it was Peter the one who founded the Christian Church in Rome. This, of course, is not apostolic teaching, as we see absolutely no record in the NT of Peter ever becoming such a singled-out authority. The NT clearly teaches that ALL the apostles are equally foundational: “And are built upon the FOUNDATION OF THE APOSTLES(plural) and prophets..” (Eph 2:19-20 KJV), “And the wall of the city had TWELVE FOUNDATIONS(not one), and in them the names of the TWELVE APOSTLES(not one) of the Lamb” (Rev 21:14 KJV). Peter himself writes two epistles and describes himself as: “an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:1), “a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 1:1). Where Apostle means the one sent/commissioned by Christ. He also calls himself “elder”(presbyteros), not even Bishop(episkopos in Greek, or overseers). Instead of elevating himself above others, he says “I am also an elder” (literally sympresbyteros, “fellow elder”) in 1 Peter 5:1. Never did he, nor anyone around him treated him as the sole authority on matters of faith. Peter received the keys of heaven with the power “to bind” & “to loose” things in earth & in heaven in Mt 16:19 because he was the first one to confess that Jesus is the Son of God (Mt 16:16), not because he had more authority than the rest of the apostles. Primacy of faith is not the same thing as primacy of rank. As the other apostles began to understand, they were also given the same keys (authority to bind and to loose) as Peter (Mt 18:18, where the “you” is plural). In fact, shortly after Peter was given the keys of heaven, the apostles were already fighting among themselves as to who is the greatest (Mt 18:1-5; Mk 9:33-37; Lk 9:46-48). So surely they weren’t aware of Peter’s supposed authority. Also, if this verse was so important in describing the unique authority given to Peter, the other gospel writers would have mentioned it as well. But they did not, they simply wrote Peter’s confession of faith & left out the part about the keys of heaven (Mt 16:16; Mk 8:29; Lk 9:20) because that was Matthew’s unique way of explaining the apostle’s authority. Before the apostles, the Pharisees and Scribes had the keys of heaven, which also had the power to “shut up the kingdom of heaven against men” (Mt 23:13 KJV). The two parallel passages describe this authority as having the “key of knowledge” in Lk 11:52, and as having the power to “shut up the kingdom of heaven against men” in Mt 23:13. Why did they have this authority? Simple, because they had access to God’s Word (common people did not have access to the Sacred Writings at the time), hence, it was up to them whether to share these “keys of knowledge” that would open up heaven to them, or to shut it down. Apostles would SEND Peter to missions (Acts 8:14). Why would others have authority to send the Pope to preach? In fact, in the very first Church Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15, we see Peter participating, not as its head, but as an elder among other elders. It was actually James, Jesus’ brother, who gave the final council verdict in Acts 15:9. Why would someone else have the final verdict when Peter is supposed to be the Pope? Around ~58AC, Paul writes the book of Romans, in which he specifically says he does not “build upon another man’s foundation” (Rom 15:20 KJV), yet he is writing to the Romans, which are supposedly under the care of Pope Peter. In Romans 16, Paul salutes all the leaders of the Roman church, yet he did not even mention Peter. Wasn’t Peter the Pope there? Of course not. There is zero evidence that Peter or Paul founded the church in Rome. Irenaeus, writing around 180AC and influenced by the mistake of Justin Martyr (misreading the statue of Simon), taught that the church of Rome was founded by both: Peter & Paul (Against Heresies, Bk 3, Ch 3, Section 2). But who do you believe, witnesses that are ~150 years after Jesus OR the apostles themselves? Because in Romans, Paul makes it clear that the church in Rome already existed even before he goes to Rome (Rom 1:10-11, 13; 15:22-24), so Irenaeus is already wrong (also, Irenaeus used “apostolic tradition” to teach that Jesus lived up to 50 years in Against Heresies Bk 2, Ch 22, section 4-6). The church of Rome was most likely founded by someone who was present at Pentecost, the Feast of Weeks (Shavuot), which required Jewish pilgrimage to the Holy City of Jerusalem. When the Holy Spirit fell on them, the text says that “strangers of Rome” (Acts 2:10 KJV) were present. Hence, it’d be easy to assume that one of these Roman/Jewish strangers actually lived in Rome, but had come to Jerusalme to celebrate the feast, and upon returning, founded the first Christian gathering in Rome. The only possible evidence to place Peter in Rome is 1 Peter 5:13 (KJV): “The church that is at BABYLON…”. Many argue that “Babylon” is code for Rome. 1 Peter was written around 60-64AC AFTER or DURING Paul’s imprisonment in Rome (Paul’s first imprisonment was in 60-62AC, see Acts 28). This means that Peter most likely went to Rome to support Paul, which is why he is writing in support of him: “Even as our beloved Paul also according to the wisdom given unto him hath written unto you; As also in all his epistles.. Which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other Scriptures, unto their own destruction” (2 Peter 3:15-16, ~64-68AC). The persecution of Christians under Emperor Nero is generally dated to 64-68AC, beginning right after the Great Fire of Rome, so it is reasonable to assume that this is when both Peter and Paul were martyred. If Catholics accept Peter’s “Babylon” as code for Rome, then they must also accept that Rome is the whore of Babylon described in Revelation 17 & 18. In those two chapters, Babylon is described as “the great whore that sitteth upon many waters”(17:1) (many waters most likely symbolizing peoples/nations), “with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication(universal idolatrous religion) and the inhabitants of the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her fornication”(17:2) (fallen into idolatry). The woman sits “upon a scarlet coloured beast”(17:3) (probably the AntiChrist or political power opposed to God). “the woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet colour, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of abominations and filthiness of her fornications” (17:4) (describing the luxuries displayed by the whore). “MYSTERY, BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH” (17:5) (she’s not just committing idolatry (fornication) by herself, she is creating other harlots). The woman is “drunken with the blood of the saints” (17:6) (the Christian martyrs persecuted by the pagan Rome & later the Roman Church). The woman sits on seven mountains (17:9) (the seven hills of Rome). This woman “is that great city, which reigneth over the kings of the earth” (17:18) (universal religion). In Chapter 18, her judgement arrives: “Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen, and is become the habitation of devils, and the hold of every foul spirit” (18:2). “For all nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth are waxed rich through the abundance of her delicacies.” (18:3) (the universal religion corrupted the whole world, and merchants got rich selling its products: penances, figurines, statues, rosaries, etc). But it will fall, and “And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more” (18:11) (her idols, incense, fine clothing, etc won’t be sold anymore). “The merchants of these things, which were made rich by her, shall stand afar off for the fear of her torment, weeping and wailing” (18:15), “Alas, alas that great city, that was clothed in fine linen, and purple, and scarlet, and decked with gold, and precious stones, and pearls!” (18:16) has fallen. “And in her was found the blood of prophets, and of saints, and of all that were slain upon the earth” (18:24) (persecution of Bible believing Christians). We do not know for certain if Babylon is Rome, but it really seems to fit in every category: (1) context in which John wrote Revelation makes sense that it would be Rome (pagan Rome); (2) Catholicism (pagan Rome mixed with Christianity) committing idolatry; (3) Catholicism keeping Rome alive through Latin & Roman hierarchy, like Pontifex Maximus(the Pope is the pagan High Priest still today); (4) Catholicism benign universal (5) Catholicism being arrayed in luxury; (6) Catholicism fornicated with the kings of all the earth; (7) Catholicism drunk with the blood of the Christians it has persecuted and murdered throughout its history, etc. For more detail on the Papacy, see note on Matthew 16:18-19.

19-20.x: A scribe, typically an affluent, respected expert of the Law, offers to follow Jesus to the other side of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus does not say “Welcome”. Instead, he issues a “reality check.” By pointing out that even animals have home while he is homeless, Jesus warns the scribe that following him does not lead to earthly prestige or security. “The Son of Man”: this is the first time in Matthew that Jesus uses this title for himself. It identifies him both with the “suffering servant” and with the glorious figure from Daniel 7:13.

Daniel 7:13 (KJV): “I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like (1)the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to (2)the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.” Many Trinitarians see two divine persons that are co-equal & co-eternal, yet they’re still somehow “one” God (notice Holy Spirit is not mentioned). A Oneness Christian sees symbolism representing the unity between the authentic human being (the Son, the Son of Man), and the only true God (Jn 17:3), the Father (the Ancient of Days). We see these two represented as one Being with one face and one name in Rev 22:3-4 (KJV): “And there shall be no more curse: but the throne of (1)God and of (2)the Lamb shall be in it; and His(singular masculine) servants shall serve Him(singular masculine): And they shall see His face(Jesus’ face, since he is the image of the invisible God); and His name(one name:Jesus, which is the only name given to men for salvation, Acts 4:10,12) shall be in their foreheads.” Rev 4:2-3 (KJV) specifically says: “ONE sat on the throne”. Isaiah saw YHWH on the throne (Isaiah 6:1). John says that Isaiah saw the glorified Jesus (who is YHWH in the flesh) (Jn 12:41). The divine Spirit (the Father) and the authentic sinless human (the Son) are both one (Jn 10:30): a temple to its Spirit (Jn 2:19), an invisible Spirit with His visible image(Col 1:15).

21-22.x: Another man asks for a delay: “Suffer me (archaic term for “allow me”) first to go and bury my father.” In Jewish culture, burying one’s father was the highest filial(Son-Father) duty. The man was likely not asking for a few hours for a funeral, but perhaps to stay at home until his father passed away or until the “secondary burial” (a year later) was complete. While Jesus clearly upholds the command to honor father and mother, the call to follow him rises above all other allegiances. Anything that hinders unqualified commitment to him and to the new covenant family of faith must be set aside. “Let the dead bury their dead”: Jesus is saying: “let those who are spiritually dead attend to the duties of the physically dead.” He is asserting that the call of the Kingdom is more urgent than even the most sacred family obligations.

29-32.x: While the disciples in the previous verses were still asking: “What manner of man is this?” (v 27), the demons knew exactly who Jesus was. “Before the time”: This reveals that the demonic realm is aware of a future “appointed time” of judgement and final defeat. They are surprised to see the Judge appearing in the middle of history to confront them. The demons begged Jesus, even in their rebellion, to enter the swine. They are completely subject to his permission. They cannot even enter an animal without his permission. “Go”: The authority of Jesus does not engage in long exorcism rituals. One word is enough to move a legion of spirits. This led to the demons possessing the swine. The destruction of the herd (about 2,000 according to Mark’s parallel account, Mk 5:13) illustrates the true intent of demonic power: destruction. Once the spirits entered the pigs, they immediately drove them to death. Why would Jesus allow the destruction of a farmer’s livelihood? (1) if the farmers were Jewish, they should not have been farming swine, as pigs were ritually unclean, so it could have served as divine correction; (2) Jesus demonstrates that the deliverance of two human beings (Mk 5:1-20 & Lk 8:26-39 mention only one demon-possessed man) made in the image of God are worth more than a herd of thousands of animals. The physical destruction of the pigs was a visible sign to the townspeople (Decapolis, Gentile region) of the magnitude of the evil that had been living in their backyard, AND the magnitude of the power that cleared it out.

33-34.x: The people of the city do not celebrate the healing of the two formerly demonized men, instead, they beg Jesus to leave. The destruction of the swine represented a major financial loss. They feared that Jesus’ presence might bring more disruption to their local economy. They were confronted by a power they did not understand and could not control. To the religious or secular mind, it is often more comfortable to live with known problems than to have them solved by a force that demands radical change. They prioritized their property (the pigs) over the restoration of their neighbors (the formerly possessed men). The city ignores the evidence, and focuses instead on their own losses.
